Science.title: Immune cells flood into the aging brain, Stanford scientists discover
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered that the aging human brain may be far less isolated from the rest of the body than once believed. Stanford researchers found that large numbers of immune cells from the blood begin entering the brain as early as middle age, where they can transform into microglia, the brain’s specialized immune cells. The finding overturns a long-standing assumption that these cells remain largely separate from the body’s immune system throughout life.

Science.title: Scientists detect a nuclear reactor’s ghostly afterglow for the first time
Science.summary: Nuclear reactors may go dark, but their fuel continues producing a faint antineutrino “glow” long after shutdown. Researchers have now detected that residual signal for the first time, finding it closely matched predictions of radioactive decay inside the reactor and nearby spent-fuel pools. The breakthrough suggests antineutrino detectors could eventually monitor reactors even when they are offline.

Sports.title: ‘That second morning at the Oval did set alarms ringing a bit …’ – our cricket correspondent Ali Martin answered your questions
Sports.summary: England’s men start their post-Bazball future next week with a three-Test series against Pakistan. Cricket correspondent Ali Martin answered your questions about omissions from the squad, new captain Joe Root’s strategy, and more TotesMcGotes asks : Would England be wise to take this opportunity - that of Root being captain presumably until the ODI World Cup is past and then Brook takes over - to move Brook to 4 and put Root at 5? Otherwise there is a good chance that Brook moves to 4 around the same time as he takes on the captaincy. Why not incentivise Brook to develop the maturity (that is lacking at times) in his game now with the added responsibility, then the captaincy would follow neatly. It also takes a bit of pressure off Root who hopefully would not be coming in to bat within 30-60mins of captaining in the field so often. As before, I would have looked to achieve this by giving Harry Brook the captaincy straight away. It’s not the worst idea now they haven’t, although with so much of the team in flux - and Root’s preference being No4 - I can see why they’ve chosen to stick with the existing order for now. It is certainly set in stone in terms of the current broadcast deal, which runs to the end of 2028 (obviously the WTC final tops this up to seven every couple of years, plus the all-too-few women’s Test matches). As for the value of each format/competition, the all-in nature of the TV deal means this is all slightly opaque. What I do know is that when the world stopped in 2020, it was Test cricket that all parties were most desperate to stage and we were told each match was worth £20m in TV money (a figure which rises significantly with crowds, corporate, sponsorship etc). Outside of World Cups, you do see interest waning in white-ball bilaterals a touch. I hope the next deal is split, so we can get a stronger sense of the breakdown. Right now I suspect Test cricket- the format most people pay their Sky subs to watch – is subsidising The Hundred… Continue reading...

Sports.title: Academic badass Amy Hunt sets sights on four golds and place in European history
Sports.summary: British sprinting sensation and Cambridge graduate with a passion for the Italian renaissance is creating a masterpiece of her own When Amy Hunt was a teenager, she was hailed by Vogue as “one of the faces to define the decade”. It has taken a few years, and several painful detours. But the 24-year-old Cambridge University graduate with a passion for the Italian renaissance is set to create an impressive masterpiece of her own. If all goes as expected this weekend, Hunt will become the first athlete in the 92-year history of the European Championships to win four gold medals over the same week. Already the 100m and 200m crowns are in the bag. And provided the baton gets around, two more will surely follow in the mixed and 4x100m relays on Saturday and Sunday. No wonder she is second favourite to be the BBC’s Sports Personality of the Year. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Vile statues, writhing liquorice and kids marooned online: Edinburgh art festival review
Culture.summary: Various venues, Edinburgh From queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like Columbo By the time you’re done with Edinburgh art festival you’ll have uncovered so many hidden stories you’ll feel like Columbo. We’re talking queer narratives, secret histories, undiscovered archives: the whole festival is a celebration of the underground and unheralded. You can’t walk into a gallery without learning about some subcultural genius or longlost creative you’ve never heard of. That’s not a bad MO for a city-wide art festival. But EAF is also a big, unwieldy, confusing thing. There are curated displays, satellite exhibitions, performances, off-site projects, and it’s impossible to figure out how any of it fits together. You’ve just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like. And you’d better like photography, because there’s a lot of it here. Continue reading...

Culture.title: A critical mauling: Brian Logan on comedy critics being portrayed as horrible snobs
Culture.summary: Two Edinburgh fringe shows feature savage send-ups of reviewers. Is this petty revenge or do they have a case? Our writer finds one ‘a hoot’ – and thinks the other let him off lightly No one ever built a statue to a critic, they say – but plenty of art gets made about them. There was Wild Bore at the Traverse a few Edinburgh fringes back, an eye-catching performance-art attack on the notion of critical authority. There was Tom Stoppard’s The Real Inspector Hound, Sheridan’s The Critic, and the 70s horror movie (later a play) Theatre of Blood , in which critics are subjected to gruesome murder at the hands of a deranged thesp. And while we’re talking unspeakable gore, one feature of Sarah Kane’s queasy play Cleansed, currently enjoying a revival , is that (in a wanton act of literary vengeance) its sadistic torturer antagonist is named after a theatre critic, Jack Tinker, who’d panned Kane’s work. Runts of the reviewing litter though we are, there’s even a sub-genre of art about comedy critics. The comic Russell Kane wrote a novel about one who was unable to laugh. Ex-critic Charlotte Runcie wrote another about a journo giving a woman a one-star review for her standup, then sleeping with her. Continue reading...
